title: The woman who whispered about an election and the novel Elizabeth Strout wrote for her
subtitle: On the morning of the Booker Prize decision, the author of The Things We Never Say offers a clue to her novel about an American history teacher: listen to what people will say only when nobody else is there.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: There was no one else in the Maine drugstore when the woman working there cupped her hands around her mouth. “I just want it over!” she told Elizabeth Strout. She meant the election. Strout agreed. She left knowing how the woman felt and still had no idea how she intended to vote.

Strout recounted the exchange in the Guardian on 7 November, two days before the Booker Prize ceremony in London. Her shortlisted novel, The Things We Never Say, is a tribute, she wrote, to people like that woman. The distinction matters to a reader opening the book expecting a political argument: the woman entrusted Strout with a feeling. She kept her ballot to herself.

The person Strout invented to carry that unease is a 57-year-old high school history teacher on the Massachusetts coast. Artie Dam is liked by his students, has a grown son and is married to Evie, a therapist. He is also desperately lonely. In an interview with the Booker Prizes, Strout traced his face to an old obituary photograph. The photograph helped her see him; the encounter in the drugstore helps explain why she wanted him to speak.

In his classroom, speech comes readily enough. When a boy imitates the way his classmate Rhonda Lazarre walks, Artie stops the lesson. He tells the class what he saw without naming the boy. The boy knows who he means. Rhonda seems not to have noticed the original slight. There is a difficult judgement in those few seconds: how does a teacher defend a girl without making her, all over again, the person everyone is looking at?

At home, the same instinct to let a name or an accusation pass can have a different effect. When Evie makes a cutting remark about a woman they know, Artie lets it go. Speaking to Literary Hub, Strout said she wanted the reader to notice both how little Artie understood about the people under discussion and that Evie had reasons of her own. A wife who listens for a living has things she chooses not to tell her husband. The reader has no more right than Artie to assume she has nothing to say.

Strout remembers what it was like to be the girl listening in. At about seven, she told the Booker Prizes, she overheard her mother discussing Harper Lee’s To Kill a Mockingbird with her father. She asked to read it. Her mother handed it over, and she finished it in two days. It is a small counterpoint to the drugstore story: sometimes the person at the edge of an adult conversation wants very much to be let in.

The Booker judges, who selected six finalists from 163 submissions, praised Strout for writing about a divided America in a way that readers on different sides could enter. The winner is due to be announced at Old Billingsgate in London on 9 November. Strout, who won the Pulitzer Prize for Olive Kitteridge, was previously shortlisted for the Booker in 2022 for Oh William!

In her Guardian account, Strout is quite explicit about her own fear for American democracy. She could easily have recruited the woman in the drugstore as a witness for her side. What gives the encounter its force, and makes it a useful way into the novel, is that she leaves the woman her secret.
